question: The CIDOC CRM class originally named 'E78 Collection' was put to a SIG vote on renaming it. Was the renaming proposal accepted, and if so what name did the SIG settle on and why?
gold_answer: Yes, the SIG approved renaming E78 Collection to E78 Curated Holding (singular, without a trailing 's'), with the change tied to resolving issue 270 at the Prato meeting in February 2016. The rationale, given by Martin Doerr during the vote, was that librarians already use 'holdings' to mean the physical copies making up library content, which supported treating the class as fundamentally about physical, curated material -- so that properties like location and destruction remain meaningful for it -- rather than about the intangible content those items carry. The vote initially ran on the plural 'Curated Holdings', but after a side debate about English usage (whether the plural reads as the collection-as-a-whole or as its individual items), several members switched their vote to the singular 'Curated Holding', which became the adopted form.
key_facts: E78 Collection was renamed to E78 Curated Holding as part of resolving issue 270.
The renaming was tied to the Prato SIG meeting in February 2016.

The stated rationale (from Martin Doerr) was that 'holdings' is the librarians' term for the physical copies of library content, supporting a physical (not purely intentional/content-based) definition of the class.
The adopted form was the singular 'Curated Holding', after some members initially voted for the plural 'Curated Holdings'.
produced_answer: Yes, the renaming was accepted. On 2016-02-05 Chryssoula Bekiari opened a formal SIG vote (issue 270) proposing to rename E78 Collection to 'E78 Curated Holdings'. Several members (George Bruseker, Martin Doerr) voted yes on the plural form, but Wolfgang Schmidle raised a linguistic objection: 'holdings' in the plural is ambiguous, sometimes meaning the collection as a whole and sometimes the individual items within it, and 'Curated Holdings' would be confusing when referring to two E78 instances. Martin Doerr agreed ('Good point! "Curated Holding" hence...') and the proposal shifted to the singular 'Curated Holding'. Stephen Stead then explicitly voted 'for Curated Holding without the S', and Pat Riva and Oyvind Eide confirmed agreement. The rationale for choosing the 'Holding(s)' terminology in the first place (over Collection, or alternatives like 'curated set'/'curated assemblage' suggested by Franco Niccolucci and Steve Stead) was Martin Doerr's explanation that librarians use 'holdings' to refer to physical copies of library contents, distinguishing holdings from informational content -- matching CRM's existing treatment of E78 as a class of physical things (needed so location and destruction can be discussed, e.g. video games in a collection must be represented by physical copies). The class was ultimately settled as 'E78 Curated Holding' (singular), which is confirmed as the current name in the ontology (v7.1.3) and by the concept chronology, which marks the 2016-02-05 episode as '[decided] Renaming E78 Collection to Curated Holding and scope clarification'.

question: The SIG discussed deprecating the actor-appellation class because its scope note failed to convincingly justify treating actor names as a distinct, recognizable kind of appellation. How did the community's position on this class evolve, and what was its fate by the following year, including any loose ends left behind?
gold_answer: The SIG largely converged on deprecating E82 Actor Appellation, because there is no reliable way to tell from the form of a name alone that it 'characteristically' belongs to an actor rather than a place or a work -- conventions about what a personal or corporate name looks like vary by culture and change over time, undermining the scope note's core claim. By the following year, a SIG member confirmed E82 had indeed been deprecated in favor of using the general E41 Appellation directly, but pointed out that dependent parts of the documentation -- the property P131 and its scope-note wording, plus references to E82 in the property hierarchy and in the entries for P1 and E39 -- had not yet been updated to match. Robert Sanderson pushed the reasoning further, arguing nearly all subclasses of E41 besides E42 Identifier add no real semantic value over plain Appellation and should likewise be deprecated.
key_facts: E82 Actor Appellation was deprecated in favor of using E41 Appellation directly.
The core objection was that the 'characteristic form' test for actor names is unreliable, since what counts as a personal or corporate name form depends on cultural convention and changes over time.

As of the following year, dependent references to E82 (including property P131 and mentions in the property hierarchy, P1, and E39) had not yet been updated in the documentation despite the deprecation.
Robert Sanderson argued the same reasoning implied nearly all subclasses of E41 (other than E42 Identifier) should also be deprecated.
produced_answer: In August 2016 (thread t0937, 'E82 Actor Appellation Issue'), Stephen Stead opened the issue: E82's scope note/examples failed to convey that an actor appellation must have a form characteristic of naming an actor, causing user confusion, and he proposed either a revised scope note or outright deprecation, favoring deprecation. The community's position hardened quickly toward removal: Dominic Oldman said he'd already assumed it would be retired; Pat Riva argued the actor/appellation distinction is not inherent to the form of a name but depends on cultural knowledge and usage context, so it can't be reliably drawn; Christian-Emil Smith Ore noted the original 2001-2002 rationale (that actor and place names have detectable, distinguishing characteristics) had been disproven; Martin Doerr voted for removing E82 and nearly all E41 subclasses except Title, Address, and Spatial Coordinates. Franco Niccolucci then proposed a general rule (R1: needed as domain/range of a property inappropriate to its superclass, or R2: a key concept in practical scope) for deciding which E41 subclasses to keep, and under that rule explicitly voted 'Leave'/'Bye bye E82' for Actor Appellation, a judgment Martin Doerr endorsed. Only Dan Matei registered dissent, saying he'd regret losing E82 since he used a subtype ('Anthroponym') in his own application. By the following year, the class's fate was effectively settled: in a June 2017 thread (t1015, 'Deprecation of Actor appellation'), Philip Carlisle wrote that 'E82 has been deprecated in favour of E41' and flagged that the property P131 (is identified by: E82 Actor Appellation) and other textual references to E82 (in the CRM Compatibility introduction, the property hierarchy, and the entries for P1 and E39) had not been updated to reflect the deprecation. Robert Sanderson agreed, adding that essentially all E41 subclasses besides E42 Identifier should likewise be deprecated as adding no new semantics. This exposed the loose end: E82 itself was treated as gone, but P131 (and related documentation cross-references) were left dangling, unresolved. That loose end persisted well past 2017 -- a January 2019 thread (t1158, 'Deprecate P78, P87?') has Robert Sanderson explicitly proposing that 'P131 / E82 also fits the same pattern, and should have the same treatment as P78 and P87' (which were being deprecated alongside E49/E44), indicating the formal property-level cleanup for E82/P131 still hadn't happened even two-plus years after the original 2016 scope-note complaint.

question: A modeller argued that the class for curated collections and the class for physical objects create a logical inconsistency, since the physical-object class's scope note already claims to cover 'all aggregates of objects... of whatever kind', yet the collections class is not classified as a subclass of it. What different fixes did SIG members propose for this, and was the class hierarchy actually changed as a result?
gold_answer: The class hierarchy was not changed. The member who raised the issue proposed making the curated-collections class (E78 Curated Holding) a subclass of Man-Made Object (so it would inherit from Physical Object through that route), or alternatively creating a new generic 'Set' class under Physical Object. Another member objected, since curated holdings must be able to include curated physical features (not just discrete objects), which would wrongly be excluded if the class were tied to Man-Made Object; he suggested using multiple instantiation instead whenever something genuinely needs to be classified as both. A third member added counter-examples -- such as a collection of dispersed structures, or curated rock art left in situ -- that would be awkward or wrong to force into the physical-object class's requirement of a single item with objective physical boundaries. The senior modeller closed the discussion by appealing to CRM's open-world, bottom-up modelling principle instead: ordinary cases like auction lots and hoards already qualify as plain physical-object aggregates, and the remaining edge cases (like objects that just happen to appear together in one photograph) simply fall outside the ontology's current scope and can be handled by an extension without touching the core hierarchy.
key_facts: No change was made to the class hierarchy as a result of this debate; E78 Curated Holding remained a non-subclass of E19 Physical Object.
One proposed fix was making E78 a subclass of E22 Man-Made Object (or introducing a new generic 'Set' class under E19), which was intended to resolve the inconsistency directly.

This was opposed on the grounds that curated holdings must be able to contain curated features (not just objects), and that some curated holdings (e.g. dispersed structures, in-situ rock art) don't satisfy E19's requirement of objective physical boundaries; multiple instantiation was proposed instead for individual overlapping cases.

The discussion was closed with an appeal to CRM's open-world/bottom-up principle rather than a hierarchy fix: ordinary aggregates like auction lots and hoards are treated as plain E19s, and edge cases are left out of scope for later extension.
produced_answer: The modeller was Robert Sanderson, who raised this in April 2017 (thread t1004, 'E78 Collection vs E19 Physical Object'): E19's scope note claims to cover 'all aggregates of objects made for functional purposes of whatever kind', E78 Curated Holding is such an aggregation, yet E78 is not a subclass of E19 (both descend independently from E18/E24), which he called a logical inconsistency ('All aggregations of objects are E19s. E78s are aggregations of objects. E78s are not E19s.'). Several different fixes were proposed. (1) Sanderson's own preferred fix: make E78 a subclass of E22 Man-Made Object, since E22 is already a subclass of both E19 and E24 -- the 'simplest change' to give E78 an E19 ancestor. He also floated a more comprehensive alternative: create a new class below E19 for 'Sets', move property P57 to it, and make E78 a child of that new class and of E24. (2) A non-hierarchy fix he also proposed: reword E78's scope note to drop the restrictive 'over time for a specific purpose... collection development plan' language, and change the clause distinguishing E78 from E19 to reference collection plans rather than physical binding/functionality. (3) Stephen Stead rejected any re-parenting: he argued E78 must be able to hold curated 'features' (not just objects), so forcing it under E22 (objects only) would wrongly exclude features; where an instance really is both an E19 and an E78, he said 'multiple instantiation is the solution, not tinkering with the class definitions'. (4) Christian-Emil Smith Ore likewise leaned toward multiple instantiation as the practical fix and, rather than committing to a hierarchy change, challenged Sanderson to formally raise a new issue with a fully worked-out, logically consistent hierarchy and draft scope notes. (5) Martin Doerr (the CRM editor) rejected the premise that there was a bug to fix at all, invoking the Open World principle: auction lots and hoards are simply E19s (they do have functionality), and things like 'the set of objects on a photo' that lack an identity condition are simply outside CRM's current scope and can be added by users without violating compatibility -- 'the CRM is NOT a data format'. No hierarchy change resulted from this thread: it is marked 'unresolved' in the concept chronology, and the current ontology (v7.1.3) still lists E78 Curated Holding as a subclass only of E24, not of E19 or E22. A later, related proposal (Issue 442, 2020, thread t1405) again left E78's parent as E24 and instead only reworded the scope note to add explicit identity criteria distinguishing E78 (identity via continuity of a development plan) from E19 (identity via the constellation of physically/functionally bound parts) -- a scope-note clarification, not a re-parenting.

question: Over the course of a year, the SIG repeatedly discussed what CIDOC CRM's class for rights actually represents -- the abstract legal concept of a right, or a specific instance of someone holding a right over an object for a bounded period -- along with how to handle joint or partial ownership shares. Did the SIG ever settle on a single answer?
gold_answer: No -- the archive shows this was never resolved. One member repeatedly pressed the SIG on whether the Right class denotes the concept of a right (which, as a Conceptual Object, cannot simply cease to exist just because its legal validity lapses) or the concrete holding of a right by a specific actor over a specific object for a limited time, and the two readings kept producing contradictory answers about things like the end of an ownership right after resale. Two members separately floated adding a new property or class to capture the period during which a right is actually in force, distinct from the right's existence as a concept, but this stayed an unadopted suggestion rather than an agreed change. The senior modeller's final word was that 'right' is simply an ambiguous natural-language term with multiple legitimate senses, that modelling joint or fractional ownership and the legal domain generally was too complex to settle by email, and that a dedicated working group would need to be restarted -- noting that an earlier such effort had already stalled once its partner organization withdrew. No resumption of that group, nor any scope-note change or new property, appears in the archive for this period.
key_facts: Whether the Right class (E30) denotes the abstract legal concept or a concrete, time-bounded holding of a right was never formally resolved -- no scope-note change or SIG vote is recorded in this period.

A proposal to add a new property or class capturing a right's period of legal validity, separate from its existence as a concept, was raised by more than one member but remained an unadopted suggestion.
The discussion also raised joint/partial ownership (e.g. two parties each holding a percentage share of a right) as unresolved, with no modelling solution agreed.

The senior modeller proposed restarting a dedicated rights-modelling working group, noting a prior effort had already stalled after a partner organization withdrew; no such group is shown reconvening.
produced_answer: No, the SIG never settled on a single answer. Starting Feb 2017 (thread t0972, 'Rights model'), Robert Sanderson asked whether E30 Right is an instance of the *holding* of a right by a specific actor over a specific object (making it look like it should be a temporally-bounded Period/Activity) or the *concept/content* of a right (consistent with its current status as a subclass of E89/E28 Conceptual Object, which never truly ceases to exist). Stephen Stead argued for the 'content of the right' reading; Martin Doerr agreed the model conflates 'the holding of the right, the content of the right, and the concept of the right' and said which of these E30 should be 'is to be discussed.' The joint/partial-ownership question (raised by Sanderson in thread t0972 on 2017-03-20, e.g. two dealers splitting profit, divorced couples splitting a shared object) was proposed to be handled via P148_has_component sub-Rights each carrying a percentage Dimension, or alternatively via a Group holding the Right (Stephen Stead's suggestion) -- but Martin Doerr explicitly declined to resolve it over email, calling it 'too complex for an e-mail discussion,' and proposed instead restarting a dormant business-transaction-modeling team effort (whose partners from the Collection Trust had already dropped out once). A related informational proposal for a new 'Right Holding' entity was floated by Athina Kritsotaki in thread t0976 (2017-03-09/10) to carry the time interval, echoing Martin's own suggestion in t0978 that the P75/P104/P105 triangle implies an unnamed 'Right Holding' state class -- but this was never adopted. The debate continued into August 2017 (thread t1019, 'End of Existence for Rights?'), where Sanderson, George Bruseker, and Stephen Stead debated whether E30's begin/end-of-existence should track the legal validity period or the conceptual-object lifespan, again without consensus; Sanderson explicitly asked 'It cannot be both. Which is it?' and no agreed answer was recorded in the thread. The formal ISSUE Martin opened ('Physical Ownership and Right', t0984, 2017-03-21) asked for use cases and scope but was left open, deferred to the never-restarted extension team. I found no later thread where the SIG reconvened and voted on or closed this issue.

question: The CIDOC CRM used to have a dedicated class for naming a specific section of a physical object (for example, 'the poop deck' of a ship). What happened to this class and the properties built on it, and how does the CRM now recommend recording such named sections?
gold_answer: The class used to represent a named section of a physical object (e.g. 'the poop deck of HMS Victory') was deprecated by the CRM SIG. As a direct consequence, the property that linked a Physical Thing to that class was also deprecated, in a vote the SIG passed unanimously in November 2018. The surviving property for locating sections, which links a Physical Thing directly to a Place, had its scope note rewritten at the same time: a named or geometrically-defined section of an object is now represented simply as a Place, identified either by a name (such as 'the poop deck of H.M.S. Victory') or by a geometry/coordinate system, rather than through a separate section-definition entity.
key_facts: E46 Section Definition was deprecated
P58 has section definition, which depended on E46, was deprecated by a unanimous SIG vote in November 2018

P59 has section (is located on or within)'s scope note was rewritten so sections are now represented directly as E53 Place instances identified by a name or a geometry, without a separate Section Definition entity
produced_answer: The class was E46 Section Definition, used to name a specific named section of a physical object (the standard example was 'poop deck of HMS Victory'), reached via P58 has section definition (E18 Physical Thing -> E46 Section Definition) and the shortcut P59 has section (E18 Physical Thing -> E53 Place). E46 Section Definition was deprecated (raised by Robert Sanderson in thread t1012, May 2017, confirmed by Martin Doerr) in favor of using appellations/place identification directly. As a consequence, in November 2018 (Issue 345) the CIDOC CRM SIG deprecated P58 has section definition entirely (voted YES unanimously, thread t1137), and revised the scope note of P59 has section (is located on or within) (thread t1139) so it is now the sole recommended way to record named sections. The new P59 scope note (proposed by Martin Doerr, agreed by the group) says the property links an E53 Place to the E18 Physical Thing it is found on/in, and that this area 'may either be identified by a name, or by a geometry in terms of a coordinate system adapted to the shape of the respective instance of E18 Physical Thing.' It explicitly gives the same ship example, noting that names for such sections are typically composed of the name of a kind of part plus the name of the object itself, e.g. 'The poop deck of H.M.S. Victory' = 'poop deck' + 'H.M.S. Victory'. So the CRM's recommendation is: drop the dedicated E46 Section Definition class/P58 property, and instead use P59 has section to link the object (E18 Physical Thing) directly to an E53 Place representing the named or geometrically-defined section.

question: The community debated removing the word 'Man' from class labels such as 'Man-Made Object'. What options were on the table, what objections were raised, and which option did the standards body actually adopt?
gold_answer: In April 2019 a proposal was made to rename the CRM's 'Man-Made' classes (covering man-made objects, features, and things) by dropping 'Man-' entirely, e.g. turning 'Man-Made Object' into 'Made Object'; replacing 'Man-' with 'Human-' was offered only as a fallback second choice. Several members objected that 'Made X' on its own was too broad and ambiguous -- it could be read as covering marks or things produced by non-human agents (one member's example was a cat's claw scratch on a painting), and 'Made Object'/'Made Thing' carried unwanted slang connotations. Others raised the cost of breaking existing URIs and labels in deployed data, and some questioned whether 'man' was really gender-biased in English at all. The SIG then put the fallback option to a formal vote, and it passed essentially unanimously, so the labels were changed to 'Human-Made Object', 'Human-Made Feature', and 'Human-Made Thing' -- the fallback option, not the original first choice of simply dropping 'Man-'.
key_facts: The original first-choice proposal was to drop 'Man-' entirely (e.g. 'Man-Made Object' to 'Made Object'), with 'Human-Made' offered only as a fallback
Objections to 'Made X' included that it was too broad/ambiguous (could include non-human-made marks) and carried unwanted connotations
The formal vote was on the fallback 'Human-Made' wording specifically, and it passed unanimously, so CRM adopted 'Human-Made Object/Feature/Thing' rather than the original 'Made X' proposal
produced_answer:
The debate began 2018-04-03 (thread t1081) when Robert Sanderson proposed renaming the gender-marked classes E22 Man-Made Object, E24 Physical Man-Made Thing, E25 Man-Made Feature and E71 Man-Made Thing. His email laid out the options: (1) simply drop 'Man-' and keep 'Made' (E22 Made Object, E25 Made Feature, E24 Physical Made Thing); (2) use 'Artificial'/'Artifact' (E22 Artifact, E25 Artificial Feature, E71 Artificial Thing); (3) 'Produced' (fits with the Production class but felt less obvious); and worse-rated alternatives 'Synthetic' (odd for natural materials), 'Manufactured' (implies industrial machinery), 'Constructed'/'Built' (implies large structures like buildings/roads). Athanasios Velios supported dropping 'Man-' and noted the issue is specific to English (other languages, e.g. Greek, don't have the problem).

The issue was revived 2019-04-12 (thread t1194), again by Robert Sanderson on behalf of the Linked Art consortium, as a formal proposal: primary choice 'Made' (Made Object/Made Feature/Made Thing), secondary choice 'Human-Made'. Objections and concerns raised in the ensuing discussion: Pierre Choffé and Franco Niccolucci argued the 'bias' was an English-specific etymological quirk and objected to the effort/cost of change (calling it 'political correctness'); Richard Light and George Bruseker raised the technical/cost concern that existing data with old URIs/labels would become inconsistent; George Bruseker and Franco Niccolucci noted 'Made' alone is ambiguous (e.g., a cat could 'make' a scratch), favoring 'Human-Made' despite it being more of a mouthful; Christian-Emil Smith Ore checked the OED to confirm 'made' wasn't overly broad; Martin Doerr stayed personally opposed, arguing 'Man-Made' was an established, useful term and that language change doesn't address real gender equity, but did not block the process and offered to run the vote; 'Artificial' had already been considered and rejected earlier because of its 'insincere/affected' secondary meaning.

On 2019-04-16 Robert Sanderson noted general consensus had shifted toward 'Human-Made' and asked to move to a vote. Martin Doerr issued a formal vote 2019-04-24 in thread t1196 ('PLEASE VOTE: Issue Man-Made'): "The proposal is to replace in all CRM labels 'Man-Made' by 'Human-Made'." Multiple SIG members (Robert Sanderson, Tony Gill, Maximilian Schich, Maja Žumer, Дарья Юрьевна Гук, and others) voted YES with no NO votes found in the retrieved messages. The ontology entry for E22 (search.py concept E22) confirms the adopted outcome: the current (v7.1.3) label is 'E22 Human-Made Object', i.e. the standards body adopted 'Human-Made' rather than plain 'Made' or 'Artificial'.

question: The CRM community discussed how to handle the fact that both a dedicated appellation entity and a plain RDF text label can be used to name the same thing. Why did the group resist simply treating the RDF text-label mechanism as directly equivalent to (a super- or sub-property of) the appellation-identification property, and what alternative did they move toward instead?
gold_answer: Martin Doerr proposed technically declaring the CRM's 'is identified by' property (P1) to be a superproperty of rdfs:label, so that a single query for P1 would also pick up names expressed as plain rdfs:label literals, and tested this in Virtuoso. Richard Light objected on technical grounds: because CRM data commonly coexists in the same triple store with unrelated RDF data that also happens to use rdfs:label, asserting that all rdfs:label statements are also P1 relationships would produce incorrect or spurious inferences over that unrelated data; he argued CRM should only define sub-classes/sub-properties of standard RDFS constructs, never super-classes/super-properties of them. Rather than resolve the P1/rdfs:label relationship by punning the two together, the discussion moved toward defining a new, separate CRM property ('has symbolic content', domain E90 Symbolic Object, range E62 String, related to rdfs:value) so that simple appellations could be given a literal value directly within the CRM's own model, without conflating CRM's identification property with the generic RDF labelling mechanism.
key_facts: Martin Doerr's proposal was to make P1 is identified by a superproperty of rdfs:label so that querying for P1 would also return rdfs:label-based names

Richard Light's objection was that this could cause spurious P1 inferences over unrelated RDF data elsewhere in the same triple store that also uses rdfs:label, and that CRM should only define sub-properties of RDFS constructs, not super-properties

Instead of linking P1 and rdfs:label directly, the SIG moved toward proposing a new property, 'has symbolic content' (domain E90 Symbolic Object, range E62 String), to represent simple appellation values as literals
produced_answer: The group repeatedly rejected making rdfs:label a sub- or super-property of P1_is_identified_by. Martin Doerr's original 2018 proposal (thread t1123, 'Issue: Solution for Dualism of E41 Appellation and rdfs:label') was to give P1 two ranges (E41 and rdf:Literal) and declare it a superproperty of rdfs:label so a single query for P1 would also return rdfs:label values. Robert Sanderson objected that this is 'punning' -- letting the same property range over both literals and resources -- which is bad RDF practice; he later (2021, thread t1495, 'RDFS, XML and more') gave the formal reason: rdfs:label is inherently a DataProperty and P1_is_identified_by an ObjectProperty, and OWL2 requires these be disjoint, so a sub/superproperty link between them is actually invalid in OWL DL. Even under plain RDFS entailment it produces nonsense: because P1's range is E41_Appellation, a subproperty assertion forces literal objects of rdfs:label to also be typed E41_Appellation (and E1_CRM_Entity, E90_Symbolic_Object, etc.), which cannot be serialized since literals cannot be subjects/typed resources. Richard Light additionally warned in 2018 that declaring P1 a superproperty of the shared, widely-used rdfs:label would contaminate unrelated RDF data in the same store (any rdfs:label anywhere would suddenly entail P1/E41 assertions), and that the differently-shaped graphs (a full P1->E41 node path vs. a bare literal) still could not be retrieved by one SPARQL pattern regardless of the sub/superproperty declaration -- so it bought nothing technically while adding risk. Mark Fichtner, George Bruseker and Nicola Carboni also pushed back, preferring E41 as a real resource. Instead of tying rdfs:label into the CRM property hierarchy, the group moved in two steps: (1) in the 2018 thread, Martin Doerr and Richard Light worked out a dedicated new CRM property for the literal content itself -- 'has symbolic content' (domain E90 Symbolic Object, range E62 String), a subproperty of rdf:value rather than of/over rdfs:label -- which became P190_has_symbolic_content, letting an E41 Appellation carry its string form without conflating the identification property with a generic RDFS label. (2) In 2021, when the same rdfs:label/P1 equivalence question resurfaced for the published RDFS file, Robert Sanderson (with Thomas Francart confirming the formal mechanism) proposed replacing the direct subPropertyOf assertion with an OWL2 property-chain axiom: 'rdfs:label owl:propertyChainAxiom (crm:P1_is_identified_by, crm:P190_has_symbolic_content)', i.e. inferring 'x P1_is_identified_by z; z a E41_Appellation; z P190_has_symbolic_content y' from 'x rdfs:label y' rather than asserting rdfs:label is itself a sub/superproperty of P1. This gives the desired inferential link between the label shortcut and the full CRM path without declaring type-incompatible properties equivalent.

question: The community considered adding a property to let two instances of the general Type class be ranked relative to each other (for example, to say a condition-report value like 'Good' outranks 'Average'). Did the group settle on this property, and if so, in what final form?
gold_answer: No, this was never settled. The idea was raised in January 2019 as a new property on E55 Type, and its proposed name changed repeatedly during discussion: first 'is conceptually greater than', then 'conceptually follows/precedes', then a suggestion of 'ranked higher than/ranked lower than'. Martin Doerr repeatedly questioned, on methodological grounds, whether such a property belonged in CRM base at all rather than being left to SKOS's existing broader/narrower relation or its OrderedCollection mechanism, and this scope question was never resolved. By June 2019 the property (again called 'is conceptually greater than') had been shifted out of CRM base into the CRMsci extension, with homework assigned to add concept-scheme context to its scope note, but the discussion ends with Martin raising further open mathematical questions about whether the relation is a partial or total order and how transitivity and part-of relations interact with it. No vote was ever taken.
key_facts: The proposed ranking property for E55 Type went through several candidate names ('is conceptually greater than', 'conceptually follows/precedes', 'ranked higher than/lower than', then back to 'is conceptually greater than')
Martin Doerr repeatedly questioned whether the property belonged in CRM base versus being left to SKOS, and this was never resolved

By mid-2019 the property had been moved from CRM base to the CRMsci extension, but no vote adopted it and open questions about its precise mathematical nature (partial vs. total order) remained unanswered
produced_answer: Yes, the group settled on adding the property, though it landed in CRMsci rather than CRMbase. Stephen Stead and Robert Sanderson raised it as a NEW ISSUE (Issue 407) in January 2019, originally proposed for CRM base as 'Pxx is conceptually greater than (is conceptually less than)', domain and range both E55 Type, quantification many-to-many (0,n:0,n), for use cases like condition-report ranks (Good > Average), map scales, and fire-hazard ratings. The name went through several rounds of debate ('conceptually follows/precedes', 'ranked higher than/lower than', 'ordinally after/before'), and Martin Doerr argued it was out of scope for CRMbase and belonged in CRMsci instead (message 2019-01-08, thread t1156). By June 2019 (thread t1219, Issue 407 update), Robert Sanderson reported agreement at the Paris SIG meeting that the property would go into CRMsci, reverting to the 'greater than/less than' naming: 'Oxx is conceptually greater than', with a revised scope note adding the notion of concept schemes/vocabularies (e.g. 'good' in a conservation-report vocabulary is greater than 'average' in the same vocabulary). A later 2022 thread (t1631) confirms this settled as a numbered CRMsci property, 'O28 is conceptually greater than (is conceptually less than)', domain/range E55 Type -- though still marked 'draft' at that point, with Martin Doerr and Athanasios Velios discussing narrowing its domain to a new subclass ('Exx Sortable Type') for a future CRMsci version rather than all of E55 Type generally.
